payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=philosophical+critiques+of+static+agent+preferences+in+reinforcement+learning+and+evolutionary+game+theory&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.5052738\", \"title\": [\"Game Theory and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: From Nash Equilibria to Evolutionary Dynamics\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5052738\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1017/s026988890500041x\", \"title\": [\"Evolutionary game theory and multi-agent reinforcement learning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>In this paper we survey the basics of reinforcement learning and (evolutionary) game theory, applied to the field of multi-agent systems. This paper contains three parts. We start with an overview on the fundamentals of reinforcement learning. Next we summarize the most important aspects of evolutionary game theory. Finally, we discuss the state-of-the-art of multi-agent reinforcement learning and the mathematical connection with evolutionary game theory.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1017/s026988890500041x\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2005, 3]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1002/cjce.24878/v1/review1\", \"title\": [\"Review for \\\"<scp>Multi‐Agent</scp> Reinforcement Learning for Process Control: Exploring the intersection between fields of Reinforcement Learning, Control Theory and Game Theory\\\"\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/cjce.24878/v1/review1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022, 12, 2]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2174/9789815322316125010012\", \"title\": [\"Reinforcement Learning in Game Theory: A Methodology for Intelligent Multi-Agent Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This paper presents a thorough methodology that makes use of cutting-edge\\nReinforcement Learning (RL) techniques to develop intelligent multi-agent systems.\\nThree phases make up the methodology: multi-agent framework, advanced learning\\ntechniques, and environment setup. Using Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), we first\\ndefined the environment by describing the reward function, state space, action space,\\nand transition probabilities. The accurate modelling of the agents' interactions with\\ntheir surroundings was made possible by this fundamental framework. To enhance\\nlearning performance and efficiency, advanced reinforcement learning techniques were\\nintroduced in phase two. To optimize the action-value function, we developed QLearning and Deep Q-Networks (DQN), incorporating their respective update rules.\\nMoreover, to directly enhance policy, policy gradient techniques were employed, such\\nas the Policy Gradient Theorem and the REINFORCE algorithm. The explorationexploitation trade-off was balanced using actor-critic approaches, where actor updates\\ndirect policy improvement and critic updates improve value function estimates. While\\ncompetitive learning uses Nash Q-learning to achieve equilibrium strategies,\\ncooperative learning concentrates on optimizing joint action-value functions.\\nEnhancing agents' capacity to learn and adapt in multi-agent contexts was the goal of\\nthis phase. All things considered, the suggested methodology combines basic and\\nsophisticated reinforcement learning techniques within an organized framework to\\ncreate multi-agent systems that are intelligent, adaptive, and able to coordinate and\\nmake decisions in challenging situations. This methodology offers a strong foundation\\nfor further investigation and implementation in multiple fields, such as distributed\\nartificial intelligence, robotics, and game theory.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2174/9789815322316125010012\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 11, 26]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "027250c2ebef43f448706e23b298ec2997f75207e9db9d71d38c6fedebb2cc05", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.5052738", "doi:10.1017/s026988890500041x", "doi:10.1002/cjce.24878/v1/review1", "doi:10.2174/9789815322316125010012"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5052738", "https://doi.org/10.1017/s026988890500041x", "https://doi.org/10.1002/cjce.24878/v1/review1", "https://doi.org/10.2174/9789815322316125010012"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

Abstract:
Cultural transmission is the domain-general social skill that allows agents to acquire and use information from each other in real-time with high fidelity and recall. In humans, it is the inheritance process that powers cumulative cultural evolution, expanding our skills, tools and knowledge across generations. We provide a method for generating zero-shot, high recall cultural transmission in artificially intelligent agents. Our agents succeed at real-time cultural transmission from humans in novel contexts without using any pre-collected human data. We identify a surprisingly simple set of ingredients sufficient for generating cultural transmission and develop an evaluation methodology for rigorously assessing it. This paves the way for cultural evolution as an algorithm for developing artificial general intelligence.
